title: What is the difference between OLTP (your production database handling fast transactions like orders/payments) and OLAP (your analytics database handling complex queries like "total sales per region last quarter"): and why you should NOT run heavy analytics on your production database?
shortTitle: Difference between OLTP and OLAP (and why not run analytics on production)
keyPoints: OLTP handles many small, fast, concurrent transactions with normalized schemas and row-oriented storage.
OLAP handles complex analytical queries over large historical data with star schemas and column-oriented storage.
OLTP uses indexes for fast point lookups; OLAP uses columnar scans for aggregations.
Running heavy analytics on the production DB starves latency-sensitive transactions of CPU, memory, and I/O.
A row-store forced to aggregate one column across millions of rows reads every column of every row, which is slow.
Separate them via ETL, ELT, or change-data-capture into a warehouse or lake.
Read replicas or streaming keep the analytics copy seconds behind for near-real-time needs.

s1_definition.oneliner: OLTP is the fast transactional counter; OLAP is the heavy analytics back office, and you keep them separate so reports never freeze live operations.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **OLTP** – Online Transaction Processing: systems that handle many small, fast, concurrent read-write transactions using normalized schemas and row-oriented storage.
- **OLAP** – Online Analytical Processing: systems that handle complex, long-running queries over large volumes of historical data using denormalized star or snowflake schemas and column-oriented storage.
- **Normalized schema** – data split into many related tables so each fact lives in one place, preventing update anomalies.
- **Star schema** – a central fact table of events surrounded by dimension tables for lookup attributes.
- **Row-oriented storage** – all columns of a row stored together, ideal for point lookups.
- **Column-oriented storage** – all values of one column stored together, ideal for aggregating a few columns across billions of rows.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India's teller counter is OLTP: hundreds of small, quick actions a second, where Rajesh withdraws cash and Priya pays rent, each touching one or two accounts and needing to be instant and correct. The bank's research department is OLAP: an analyst asks "what was total spend per branch last quarter", a heavy question scanning millions of records. If you forced the analyst to run that giant report on the live teller system, every customer at the counter would be stuck waiting. So the bank copies data into a separate analytics system where big questions run without freezing the counter.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  OLTP vs OLAP
  ────────────

  OLTP (Row-Oriented)                OLAP (Column-Oriented)
  ┌──────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────┐
  │ row1: id|amt|dt  │               │ id:  1,2,3,4,5.. │
  │ row2: id|amt|dt  │               │ amt: 100,200,... │
  │ row3: id|amt|dt  │               │ dt:  Oct,Oct,... │
  │ row4: id|amt|dt  │               │                  │
  │ (all cols together)│              │ (each col stored │
  │                  │               │  separately)     │
  └──────────────────┘               └──────────────────┘
  Fast point read/write              Fast column scan/aggregate
```

```text
  Separation Pattern
  ──────────────────
  ┌──────────┐  CDC/ETL  ┌───────────┐
  │   OLTP   │─────────▶│   OLAP    │
  │ (Postgres)│          │(Redshift) │
  │          │          │           │
  │ Rajesh's │          │ Total per │
  │ payment  │          │ branch    │
  │ (2 ms)   │          │ (8 sec)   │
  └──────────┘          └───────────┘
  Customer-facing         Analyst-facing
  Never degraded          Scales independently
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
OLTP and OLAP are two system types tuned for opposite workloads. OLTP handles many small, fast, concurrent transactions like placing orders or processing payments. It uses normalized schemas so each fact lives in one place, row-oriented storage because you touch whole single rows, indexes for fast point lookups, and ACID transactions for correctness. OLAP handles a smaller number of very heavy queries over large volumes of historical data. It uses denormalized star or snowflake schemas, column-oriented storage because you aggregate a few columns across billions of rows, and it is tuned for large scans rather than point writes.

The reason you must not run heavy analytics on the production OLTP database is resource contention plus a design mismatch. A giant analytical scan consumes CPU, memory, and I/O and can hold locks or saturate the cache, which starves the small transactions, so a withdrawal that normally takes a few milliseconds suddenly takes seconds or times out. The storage model is also wrong, because a row store forced to aggregate one column across millions of rows must read every column of every row.

The fix is to separate them by moving data from OLTP into an OLAP warehouse or lake through an ETL or ELT pipeline or a change-data-capture stream, which isolates the workloads so analytics scales independently and never degrades customer-facing latency. For near-real-time needs you can use read replicas or streaming so the analytics copy is only seconds behind, and HTAP systems try to blend both, but in a bank the safest conventional pattern is clear separation.

In a banking context at the National Bank of India, Rajesh's and Priya's payments were fast single-row writes on the production OLTP database, a CDC sync copied committed transactions into the analytics warehouse, and heavy reports like total spend per branch ran entirely on OLAP. That way an analyst's quarterly report could never slow down a customer's payment.

Remember one sentence: OLTP handles fast point transactions, OLAP handles heavy analytical scans, and you separate them so reports never freeze live operations.
